title: RCUK welcomes historic ICJ ruling on Rohingya genocide and calls for international action to implement it
excerpt: 20 November 2026 The Rohingya Centre of United Kingdom (RCUK) welcomes the judgment of the International Court of Justice in The Gambia v. Myanmar. The Gambia brought the case on…
content:
20 November 2026

The Rohingya Centre of United Kingdom (RCUK) welcomes the judgment of the International Court of Justice in The Gambia v. Myanmar. The Gambia brought the case on 11 November 2019, accusing Myanmar of genocide against the Rohingya in breach of the Genocide Convention.

The judgment

On 19 November 2026, the Court found, by nine votes to six, that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine State during the 2017 clearance operations, in violation of the Genocide Convention. This is the first time the Court has found that a state itself committed genocide. The judgment is final, without appeal and binding on the parties.

The Court also found that Myanmar:

  • failed to prevent genocide by individuals acting alongside its security forces
  • failed to punish genocide and related acts
  • failed to pass the laws needed to give effect to the Convention
  • breached the Court’s provisional measures order of January 2020 by failing to preserve evidence.

What the Court ordered

The Court ordered Myanmar to:

  • pass legislation giving full effect to the Convention
  • investigate everyone reasonably suspected of genocide and related acts in the 2017 operations, and prosecute and punish them where warranted
  • provide guarantees that these violations will not be repeated
  • adopt measures of restitution, including the safe, voluntary and dignified return of displaced Rohingya to their homes and the reunification of families, whether they were displaced inside Myanmar or abroad
  • compensate the Rohingya group and its members for the harm caused.

Myanmar must report to the Court within two years on the restitution it has carried out and on compensation. The Court will then decide the amount and form of reparation.

Appreciation

RCUK thanks the Government of The Gambia and its legal team for bringing and pursuing this case, the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation for its support, and the eleven states that intervened: Belgium, Canada, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Denmark, France, Germany, Ireland, the Maldives, the Netherlands, Slovenia and the United Kingdom. RCUK also recognises the survivors, witnesses, investigators and Rohingya organisers whose evidence and persistence made this judgment possible.

“This judgment settles the question of what happened to our people. It is now a matter of international law, not opinion. The Court has also set out what Myanmar owes: prosecutions, return, reunited families and compensation. The question now is whether the world makes sure it is delivered. We provided the evidence. We intend to be at the table for what follows.” — Mohammed Amin, CEO, RCUK

From judgment to implementation

The Court has no means of enforcing its decisions. Myanmar has already been found in breach of the Court’s 2020 order to preserve evidence, so the international community cannot rely on its goodwill. Every state party to the Genocide Convention has committed to prevent and punish genocide.

RCUK calls on:

  • the Security Council to adopt measures that give effect to the judgment, including referral of the situation in Myanmar to the International Criminal Court
  • the United Nations to monitor Myanmar’s compliance during the two-year reporting period and to report publicly on its progress
  • all member states, including those in Asia and the members of ASEAN, to recognise the judgment by name and support its implementation
  • states with relevant influence to impose further targeted sanctions on the revenue, arms and jet fuel that reach Myanmar’s military
  • donors to secure sustained funding for the Rohingya response in Bangladesh, so that Bangladesh does not carry this responsibility alone
  • donors, UN agencies and international NGOs to invest directly in Rohingya-led organisations and initiatives, strengthening their capacity to lead their own response and reducing long-term dependence on external aid.

Return and reparation

The return ordered by the Court can only last if the Arakanese Rohingya regain full citizenship, equal rights, freedom of movement and access to land. All armed actors in Arakan, state and non-state, including the Arakan Army, must respect these rights and must not obstruct safe return. Decisions about return and compensation must not be made without the people they are owed to.

The United Kingdom

RCUK welcomes the statement by the Foreign Secretary, the Rt Hon Ed Miliband MP. It confirms the expulsion of Myanmar’s Defence Attaché, the summoning of Myanmar’s Chargé d’Affaires and an urgent call for a Security Council session on the judgment. RCUK also welcomes the UK Government’s commitment to set out further action in the coming days, and the letter from Imran Hussain MP, Chair of the APPG on the Rohingya, to the Foreign Secretary.

RCUK values its engagement with the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office, including on education and humanitarian support for Rohingya refugees. It recognises the UK’s sustained humanitarian contribution to the Rohingya response, which the FCDO has put at £452 million.

As the penholder on Myanmar at the Security Council and one of the states that intervened in this case, the UK is well placed to lead. As it decides on its further action, RCUK calls on the UK Government to:

  • use its role as penholder to lead the Security Council action set out above and maintain UK humanitarian funding and use its diplomatic influence to mobilise other donors, partners and multilateral institutions
  • protect essential humanitarian provision, particularly food assistance, cooking fuel, healthcare, shelter, quality education and livelihoods, while addressing serious protection and security concerns in the camps, especially for women and girls
  • support Rohingya-led education and opportunities for young Rohingya people, including RCUK’s work, primary and secondary education, teacher training, skills development and a UK higher education scholarship programme.

Looking ahead

The Rohingya must remain at the centre of decisions affecting their lives, dignity and future. RCUK will continue to bring the views of Rohingya people in the UK to the Government, Parliament and international partners as the judgment is implemented, drawing on its links with the Rohingya community in the UK and Rohingya communities in Cox’s Bazar.

The Court’s press release (No. 2026/30) and the full judgment are available at icj-cij.org.

About RCUK

The Rohingya Centre of United Kingdom (RCUK) is a Rohingya-led organisation that works on justice and accountability, alongside developing sustainable, community-driven solutions to the Rohingya crisis. Based in the United Kingdom, RCUK connects grassroots knowledge with international action to enable Rohingya people to live with dignity, rights and opportunity.

title: ICJ to Rule on Rohingya Genocide Case Against Myanmar
excerpt: Bradford, United Kingdom | 5 November 2026 On 3 November 2026, the International Court of Justice (ICJ), the United Nations’ highest court, announced that it will deliver its judgment on…
content:
Bradford, United Kingdom | 5 November 2026

On 3 November 2026, the International Court of Justice (ICJ), the United Nations’ highest court, announced that it will deliver its judgment on Thursday 19 November 2026 in the case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar on 11 November 2019 under the Genocide Convention.

The Rohingya Centre of United Kingdom (RCUK) regards 19 November as a historic date for the Arakanese Rohingya people: the day the world’s highest court will give its judgment on the atrocities committed against them.

Why this case matters

For decades, the Myanmar military’s crimes against the Rohingya people went unpunished. No court examined them, and no one was held to account. That impunity allowed the abuses to continue and to grow, culminating in the atrocities of 2016 and 2017.

The Gambia’s case changed this. Brought with the support of the 57 member states of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, it was the first time a state with no direct connection to alleged genocide used the Genocide Convention to bring another state before the ICJ. It established that preventing genocide is the responsibility of every state that has signed the Convention.

This is a case between two states, not a criminal trial, and no individual will be convicted or imprisoned. The Court’s judgment will be final, with no appeal.

The proceedings so far

  • 23 January 2020: The Court unanimously ordered Myanmar to take all measures within its power to prevent genocidal acts against the Rohingya people, to ensure that its military and any irregular armed units did not commit them, and to preserve evidence. It required Myanmar to report regularly on its compliance. Myanmar submitted twelve reports; The Gambia has maintained that none of them shows that Myanmar complied.
  • 22 July 2022: The Court rejected all of Myanmar’s objections, including its claim that The Gambia was acting as a proxy for the OIC. It held that every state party shares a common interest in preventing and punishing genocide, and that The Gambia therefore had the right to bring the case.
  • 2023–2024: The parties exchanged written arguments, with Myanmar filing its final submission in December 2024.
  • 2024–2025: The Court admitted eleven states as interveners on how the Convention should be interpreted: Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom and the Maldives in July 2024, and Slovenia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Belgium and Ireland in July 2025.
  • 12–29 January 2026: The Court held public hearings on the merits, including the examination of three witnesses and one expert called by The Gambia, and one witness called by Myanmar. On 29 January 2026, the Court began its deliberations.

What The Gambia is asking the Court

The Gambia asks the Court to declare that Myanmar breached the Genocide Convention by committing genocide, conspiring to commit genocide, failing to prevent genocide and failing to punish those responsible, and that Myanmar failed to comply with the Court’s 2020 order.

It asks the Court to order Myanmar to end all violations, to make genocide a crime under its own law, to put those suspected of genocide on trial, and to stop public incitement to genocide.

It also asks for reparation for Rohingya victims, including:

  • the safe and dignified return of those forced from their homes;
  • the return or replacement of land and property;
  • the reunification of separated families;
  • physical and psychological rehabilitation for survivors;
  • the search for those who have disappeared, and the recovery and reburial of those killed in accordance with Rohingya religious and cultural practice;
  • protection from discrimination and persecution, including the right of the Rohingya to identify as Rohingya, and freedom of movement, residence and work; and
  • compensation where return and restitution are not possible.

Finally, it asks for guarantees that the violations will not be repeated.

For the Arakanese Rohingya, these requests describe what justice would mean in practice: returning home, recovering what was taken, finding the missing, and being recognised by name.

Myanmar denies that its operations were genocidal, describing them as counter-terrorism operations, and disputes The Gambia’s right to claim reparation on behalf of the Rohingya people.

The Arakanese Rohingya

The Rohingya people are a predominantly Muslim whose homeland is Arakan (Rakhine State) in western Myanmar now. Since the military seized power in 1962, the Myanmar state has denied them freedom of movement and basic rights, and most Rohingya people were stripped of citizenship under Myanmar’s 1982 Citizenship Law.

The Rohingya people have been driven from Arakan in successive waves. Around 200,000 fled to Bangladesh in 1978, and around 250,000 in 1991–92. In 2012, violence in Arakan forced more than 140,000 Rohingya people into camps inside Myanmar. In 2016 and 2017, Myanmar’s security forces carried out a campaign of killings, rape and arson that forced more than 700,000 people to flee to Bangladesh. Today, more than 1.2 million Rohingya people live in the camps of Cox’s Bazar, the largest refugee settlement in the world.

The Bradford Rohingya community

Bradford is home to the largest Rohingya community in the United Kingdom and one of the largest in Europe. Many of its members lived through the persecution and displacement of 1978 and the 1990s, and spent years as refugees before arriving in the UK with the support of UNHCR and the UK’s refugee resettlement programme. Many still have family members in the camps of Cox’s Bazar.

The community has followed this case from the beginning. Members of the Bradford Rohingya community attended the first hearings in The Hague in December 2019 and the hearings on the merits in January 2026, and will attend the reading of the judgment at the Peace Palace on 19 November.

Anwara Begum, who spent more than thirty years in refugee camps in Bangladesh before settling in Bradford, said:

“I lost my father to the military in the 1990s. I watched them shoot him. What happened to my family has happened to thousands of Rohingya families, again and again, for as long as I can remember. They treated us as less than human. I have seen generation after generation of our people driven from their homes. This case is for all of them. I am nervous about 19 November, but I hope the world will finally say that what was done to the Rohingya was inhumane and a war crime, and that those responsible must answer for it.”

Deen Mohammed Noori, a former community leader, said:

“My elderly parents are still in the camps in Bangladesh, still living with what the military did to our family and our people. Millions of Rohingya are scattered across neighbouring countries, stuck in limbo. We exist as people, but not in any system. That erasure was deliberate: a people with no records leaves no evidence, and that is how the military has escaped justice again and again. I have attended every hearing in this case for my parents, and I will be there for them again on 19 November. I hope the judgment brings meaningful justice to us.”

What the judgment could mean

If the Court finds that Myanmar committed genocide, the world’s highest court will have confirmed what the Rohingya people have lived through: not a “crisis” or “counter-terrorism”, but an attempt to destroy a people. No state has ever been found by the ICJ to have committed genocide itself; Myanmar would be the first. A narrower ruling, that Myanmar failed to prevent or punish genocide, or did not comply with the Court’s 2020 order, would still establish that Myanmar broke international law in its treatment of the Rohingya people.

Whatever the outcome, the judgment will stand as a permanent legal record and a foundation for every effort that follows: the International Criminal Court’s investigation, the case in Argentina, and the Rohingya people’s claims to return, citizenship and reparation.

Under the UN Charter, Myanmar is legally bound to comply with the judgment. The Court has no means of enforcing it directly. If Myanmar does not comply, The Gambia can refer the matter to the UN Security Council, which has the power to make recommendations or decide on measures to give effect to the judgment. The Council has never used this power. The UN General Assembly can also call on Myanmar to comply, and individual governments can apply pressure of their own. Whether the judgment brings real change to the lives of the Rohingya people depends on what governments do next.

Standing together on 19 November

RCUK recognises that the day will be painful for many survivors and families, and encourages members of the community to follow it together. RCUK also thanks its supporters and allies, and asks them to continue standing with the Rohingya people after 19 November.

Mohammed Amin, Chief Executive Officer of RCUK, said:

“For our community, 19 November will be a day of reckoning. We are grateful to The Gambia for bringing this case, to the member states of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation for supporting it, to the states that intervened, in particular the United Kingdom, and to Bangladesh, which has sheltered the Rohingya people since 1978. The Court will decide the question of law. What follows must be action, so that justice reaches every Rohingya people driven from their home, and peace and stability return to Arakan, ending a crisis that has lasted decades and concerns us all as human beings.”

Following the judgment

  • When: Thursday 19 November 2026, 10 a.m. in The Hague (9 a.m. UK time).
  • Online: streamed live in English and French on the ICJ website (icj-cij.org) and UN Web TV (webtv.un.org). A recording will be available afterwards.
  • In person: the Peace Palace, The Hague. Only 15 public seats are available, on a first-come, first-served basis, with no advance booking. Visitors should arrive at the main gate at least 40 minutes early with valid identification.

The Court reads its reasoning first, and its decisions on each claim come at the end.

title: Rohingya communities take the lead on education in Cox’s Bazar as new programme receives government approval
excerpt: Diaspora-led initiative to open first school in Camp 18 and develop pathways to vocational and higher education Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh — 18 October 2026 For the first time, a Rohingya…
content:
Diaspora-led initiative to open first school in Camp 18 and develop pathways to vocational and higher education

Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh — 18 October 2026

For the first time, a Rohingya diaspora organisation has secured government approval to run an education programme in the Rohingya refugee camps that is designed, owned and delivered by the Rohingya community itself.

On 15 October 2026, the NGO Affairs Bureau, Prime Minister’s Office, Government of Bangladesh, approved the Educate Rohingya Children Program (ERCP). It will be delivered by Pulse Bangladesh Society, a registered Bangladeshi organisation, with the Rohingya Centre of United Kingdom (RCUK) as programme owner and funder. The approval follows a visit by an RCUK delegation to Cox’s Bazar from 28 August to 6 October 2026.

“Last year we came with a plan; this year we returned to put it into practice,” said Mohammed Amin, Chief Executive Officer of RCUK. “Education is a right and a foundation for dignity. Our aim is to support Rohingya communities to build an education system they can sustain themselves, working alongside the Government of Bangladesh and all partners. With quality education and practical skills, Rohingya young people can contribute to their community today and prepare for a safe, voluntary and dignified return home.”

Why it matters now

Bangladesh hosts more than 1.2 million Rohingya refugees, according to UNHCR. In June 2025, funding shortfalls led to the closure of more than 6,400 learning centres in the camps, affecting around 300,000 children. Since then, Rohingya families and teachers have kept learning going themselves, often with little support.

RCUK’s programme builds on that determination. Rather than depending on short-term funding, it invests in Rohingya teachers, parents and young people, building the skills and confidence they need to lead their own lives and to rebuild their communities on a safe, voluntary and dignified return to Arakan. The first 32 Rohingya teachers have already been trained and certified, from more than 500 who registered interest. RCUK’s first primary school is now opening in Camp 18, teaching Rohingya, Burmese, English, Mathematics, Science, Islamic Studies, Social Studies, and Games and Physical Education.

One year from pilot to programme

RCUK’s first delegation visited the camps in September 2025 and introduced a pilot for community-led education. Over the past year, RCUK has developed the Rohingya Education System, a structured curriculum framework from early childhood to secondary level, and built a system to monitor learning and the use of resources.

This year’s delegation was led by Mohammed Amin and included Abdu Shukkur, Regional Director (Germany); Professor Mohammed Shafiullah, Managing Director of the Rohingya Education System (Bangladesh); and Hafez Mohammed Abu Taher, General Camps Supervisor (Cox’s Bazar). It turned the framework into a working programme. On 10 September 2026, RCUK signed a Partnership Memorandum of Understanding with Pulse Bangladesh Society in Cox’s Bazar.

The delegation also met officials at the Office of the Refugee Relief and Repatriation Commissioner (RRRC), joined by Pulse, the RCUK team on the ground and fellow Rohingya diaspora organisations. All those present shared the view that structured, skills-based education is central to the future of Rohingya people. In the camps, the delegation held discussions with community organisations and teachers, whose views have shaped the programme’s next steps.

Beyond the classroom

Primary education is only the start. The delegation explored pathways to higher education for Rohingya youth, and practical vocational training centres where young people can learn skills and earn a livelihood.

As part of this work, the delegation met Sadat Khan, Associate Professor and Director of the International Affairs Office at Premier University, Chittagong. They discussed how RCUK’s higher education pathway could be developed, including facilities for its proposed University of Arakan (UoA), an online initiative for higher studies.

The delegation was honoured to visit the Rohang Heritage Centre in Cox’s Bazar, which safeguards Rohingya history, culture and identity for future generations. RCUK thanks the camp authorities and the Camp-in-Charge for supporting this initiative.

A contribution to global goals

The programme supports Sustainable Development Goal 4, on inclusive and equitable quality education for all, and the Global Compact on Refugees’ objective of enhancing refugee self-reliance. It is designed to complement the efforts of the Government of Bangladesh, UN agencies and humanitarian partners.

RCUK expresses its sincere gratitude to the Government and people of Bangladesh, and to the host communities of Cox’s Bazar, for the considerable responsibility they have carried in hosting Rohingya refugees since 1978, and especially since 2017, when the camps in Cox’s Bazar became the world’s largest refugee camp. It also thanks the RRRC, the NGO Affairs Bureau, Pulse Bangladesh Society, the National Education Union, and all other partners and individuals who have contributed to this work.

What comes next

Over the coming year, RCUK and Pulse will open the Camp 18 school, train the next cohort of Rohingya teachers and develop proposals for vocational and higher education. RCUK will publish a progress report in September 2027.

RCUK calls on governments, UN agencies, donors and partners to support Rohingya-led education through predictable, multi-year funding; to work together on recognised pathways to secondary, vocational and higher education; and to invest in the capacity of Rohingya communities to lead their own education.

title: Statement on the 3 June 2012 Violence in Arakan
excerpt: 3 June 2026 – Bradford, United Kingdom Rohingya Centre of United Kingdom (RCUK) issues this statement on the International Day of Solidarity with the Rohingya People, marking the tragic events…
content:
3 June 2026 – Bradford, United Kingdom

Rohingya Centre of United Kingdom (RCUK) issues this statement on the International Day of Solidarity with the Rohingya People, marking the tragic events of 3 June 2012, a date of deep significance for Rohingya communities worldwide.

On this day in 2012, ten Rohingya travellers were killed in Taungup township while returning home by bus. This incident triggered widespread violence across Arakan (Rakhine) State, leading to the destruction of Rohingya neighbourhoods, mass displacement, and long‑term humanitarian suffering.

According to documented reports by international human rights organisations, tens of thousands of Rohingya were forced from their homes, many of whom remain displaced today in internally displaced persons (IDP) camps within Arakan State and in refugee camps in Bangladesh.

The events of 3 June 2012 marked a turning point in the modern history of the Rohingya people. The violence that followed deepened existing vulnerabilities, entrenched segregation, and contributed to the conditions that later culminated in genocide and the mass displacement of 2016 and 2017.

Historical Responsibility and Humanitarian Impact

The tragedy of 3 June 2012 cannot be understood in isolation. It forms part of a broader historical pattern of discrimination, statelessness, and vulnerability affecting the Rohingya people for decades.

International organisations including the United Nations, Human Rights Watch, and Amnesty International have documented the severe humanitarian consequences that followed the 2012 violence. Entire communities were uprooted, confined to restricted areas, and denied basic rights such as freedom of movement, access to livelihoods, and essential services.

Today, nearly nine years after the 2017 mass displacement, almost 1.5 million Rohingya refugees remain in Bangladesh, living in the world’s largest refugee settlement. Conditions remain extremely challenging, with overcrowding, food insecurity, disease, and limited access to education and livelihoods.

UNHCR Funding Appeal and Humanitarian Crisis

In its latest briefing on 2 June 2026, UNHCR warned that the world must not forget the Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh. The UN and partners have launched a US$710.5 million hyper‑prioritised appeal, now only 60 per cent funded, despite rising needs and the arrival of 150,000 new refugees fleeing renewed violence in Arakan State since early 2024.

Funding shortages have already forced reductions in food, healthcare, protection services, and education, leaving vulnerable groups including women, girls, older people, and people with disabilities at heightened risk. UNHCR warns that without sustained international support, conditions will deteriorate further, driving more Rohingya people to desperate and dangerous journeys across the region.

This moment demands renewed global solidarity, including investment in community‑based initiatives that strengthen resilience, dignity, and long‑term wellbeing for Rohingya families. The suffering of the Rohingya people must not be ignored, denied, or erased.

RCUK’s Call to the International Community

RCUK calls upon governments, human rights organisations, historians, policy makers, and civil society partners to acknowledge the historical realities faced by the Rohingya people with fairness, balance, and factual integrity. Selective narratives, historical denial, and misinformation undermine justice and obstruct genuine reconciliation.

RCUK rejects all forms of extremism, atrocities, and violence targeting civilians, regardless of ethnicity or religion. We support peaceful coexistence, humanitarian assistance, and the protection of all communities affected by conflict in Arakan. As a community‑based organisation, RCUK emphasises the importance of investing in grassroots initiatives that strengthen resilience, dignity, and long‑term wellbeing for Rohingya people in the UK, in the diaspora, and globally.

Conclusion

Today, we honour the memory of the Rohingya victims of 3 June 2012.
We reaffirm our commitment to:

  • historical truth
  • human dignity
  • justice and accountability
  • the protection of vulnerable communities
  • the preservation of Rohingya identity and heritage

On this International Day of Solidarity with the Rohingya People,
we remember, we honour, and we stand together.

title: RCUK Congratulates H.E. Dr Khalilur Rahman on His Election as President of the UN General Assembly
excerpt: Bradford, United Kingdom – 02 June 2026 Mohammed Amin, Chief Executive Officer of the Rohingya Centre of the United Kingdom (RCUK), conveys his sincere congratulations to the Government of the…
content:
Bradford, United Kingdom – 02 June 2026

Mohammed Amin, Chief Executive Officer of the Rohingya Centre of the United Kingdom (RCUK), conveys his sincere congratulations to the Government of the People’s Republic of Bangladesh and to H.E. Dr Khalilur Rahman, Honourable Minister of Foreign Affairs, on his election as President of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly.

The CEO extends his best wishes to H.E. Dr Khalilur Rahman for success in the discharge of his duties, expressing confidence that his leadership of the General Assembly will contribute to strengthening multilateral cooperation and addressing shared challenges affecting all communities in Arakan (Rakhine State). He notes that Dr Rahman’s diplomatic experience and longstanding engagement in international affairs will be valuable in this regard.

Mr Amin acknowledges Bangladesh’s continued role in hosting over 1.5 million displaced Rohingya refugees, and affirms his hope that Dr Rahman’s presidency will support efforts aimed at advancing protection, stability, and durable solutions for Rohingya people. He notes that the situation in Arakan remains shaped by longstanding and complex challenges that have disproportionately affected Rohingya people, underscoring the importance of approaches that prioritise humanitarian support, accountability, community‑centred development, and sustainable, long‑term solutions for the region.

The CEO further reaffirms RCUK’s commitment to constructive engagement with international partners in the promotion of peace, justice, sustainable development, and the dignity of Rohingya people and all affected communities.

title: RCUK Hosts UN IIMM Delegation for Justice and Accountability Dialogue in Bradford
excerpt: Bradford, United Kingdom – The Rohingya Centre UK (RCUK) successfully hosted the Justice & Accountability Dialogue & Rohingya Community Reception and Iftar on 6 March 2026 at the Banqueting Hall,…
content:
Bradford, United Kingdom – The Rohingya Centre UK (RCUK) successfully hosted the Justice & Accountability Dialogue & Rohingya Community Reception and Iftar on 6 March 2026 at the Banqueting Hall, City Hall, Bradford. The event brought together Rohingya community members, civil society organisations, parliamentarians, educators, faith leaders, and international justice partners to discuss justice, accountability, and the long-term resilience of the Rohingya people.

RCUK welcomed the delegation from the United Nations Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar (IIMM), including Mr Nicholas Koumjian, Head of the Mechanism, and Ms Kaoru Okuizumi, Deputy Head. Mr Koumjian outlined the Mechanism’s mandate from the UN Human Rights Council to collect and preserve evidence of serious international crimes committed in Myanmar since 2011.

He provided updates on key judicial processes currently underway:

  • Argentina: Investigation resulting in arrest warrants for 25 individuals responsible for crimes against the Rohingya.
  • International Criminal Court (ICC): Evidence submitted to support arrest warrant requests against Myanmar military leadership.
  • International Court of Justice (ICJ): Case filed by Gambia under the Genocide Convention, with oral hearings held in January 2026 and a decision expected later this year.

Mr Koumjian also highlighted ongoing resource and financial challenges facing the Mechanism. RCUK called on the UK Government, including relevant partners, to continue supporting IIMM’s work, ensuring thorough, independent investigations and sustained international accountability.

Dr Mohammed Khubybe, Chief Operating Officer of RCUK, delivered the keynote address, emphasising that the Rohingya crisis is a political issue, driven by decades of systemic discrimination, persecution, and the 2017 genocidal campaign, rather than solely a humanitarian emergency. He noted that meaningful justice requires credible evidence, accountability mechanisms, and legal processes to prevent impunity. He also highlighted the importance of justice and opportunity for Rohingya children and families so that future conditions may allow for safe and dignified return to their homeland.

Imran Hussain MP recognised Bradford as a city of sanctuary and highlighted the global significance of IIMM’s work. He reaffirmed his commitment to international justice processes, stressing that perpetrators of genocide, war crimes, and ethnic cleansing must be held accountable.

Hazel Danson, National Treasurer of the National Education Union (NEU), outlined support for Rohingya-led education initiatives, including ongoing funding, teacher recruitment and training in refugee camps. The partnership aims to enable Rohingya educators to lead the education of their own children in a sustainable and meaningful way.

The evening also featured:

  • Rohingya Photo Exhibition, showcasing the history, culture, and lived experiences of the Rohingya people, highlighting resilience and preserving cultural heritage.
  • The programme was hosted by Fatima Mahmood from the Race Equality Network.
  • Qur’an recitation by Essa Saho, Madrasah Teacher
  • Civil society perspectives from Deen Mohammed Noori, Chairman of the Arakan Rohingya Organisation UK
  • Youth perspectives from young Rohingya community members
  • Opening Iftar and Dua led by Dr Qader Khan, Teacher at Umm Ul Qura Islamic Centre, Bradford

The programme concluded with closing remarks from Mohammed Amin, CEO of RCUK, reaffirming the organisation’s commitment to sustainable, community-led systems in education, social support, and governance. He stressed the importance of empowering Rohingya-led initiatives in education, social support, and governance, enabling communities to build long-term resilience and manage their own future beyond short-term humanitarian aid.

“This event shows the resilience and agency of the Rohingya community and the importance of international partnerships in supporting justice and accountability,” said Mohammed Amin. “We call on the UK Government to continue supporting IIMM’s essential work and to empower Rohingya-led initiatives that deliver lasting impact. The Rohingya crisis is political; sustainable solutions require political engagement, global solidarity, and enabling directly our communities to secure their own future.”

title: RCUK Statement on the Death of Nurul Amin Shah Alam
excerpt: The Rohingya Centre of United Kingdom (RCUK) is deeply saddened by the death of Nurul Amin Shah Alam, a 56‑year‑old Rohingya genocide survivor from Myanmar, who was found deceased in…
content:
The Rohingya Centre of United Kingdom (RCUK) is deeply saddened by the death of Nurul Amin Shah Alam, a 56‑year‑old Rohingya genocide survivor from Myanmar, who was found deceased in Buffalo, New York, on 24 February 2026.

Mr. Shah Alam and his family were resettled in the United States through the UN Refugee Resettlement Programme after fleeing persecution in Myanmar’s Rakhine State. Like many Rohingya families displaced by violence recognised by the United States as genocide, they arrived seeking safety, dignity, and stability.

In 2025, shortly after his arrival, Mr. Shah Alam was arrested following what his family described as a misunderstanding. Nearly blind and unable to speak English, he had been using a curtain rod as a walking stick when he became lost and entered private property. Unable to understand police instructions, he was taken into custody. He remained at the Erie County Holding Center for much of the following year while his case proceeded, ultimately concluding with a misdemeanor plea agreement.

During his detention, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) issued an immigration detainer requesting notification prior to his release. On 19 February 2026, after his family posted bail, the Erie County Sheriff’s Office contacted U.S. Border Patrol in response to that detainer. Federal officials later confirmed that Mr. Shah Alam had lawfully entered the United States as a refugee and was not subject to removal.

Instead of being returned home, Mr. Shah Alam was transported by Border Patrol agents and left at a coffee shop miles away from his residence. His family and attorney report that they were not informed of his location. Mr. Shah Alam did not have a phone, could not read or write, and was navigating freezing winter conditions.

He was reported missing. On 24 February, five days after his release, he was found unresponsive on a Buffalo street approximately four miles from where he had been left. Buffalo Police have confirmed that homicide detectives are investigating the circumstances and timeline leading to his death.

New York State Senator Sean Ryan described the death as “preventable” and criticised what he called “inhumane” decision‑making by federal immigration authorities, noting that a vulnerable man nearly blind and unable to speak English — was left alone on a cold winter night without being placed in a safe and secure location.

RCUK CEO Mohammed Amin stated:

“Nurul Amin Shah Alam survived genocide and sought safety in a country that promised protection. The events between his release on February 19 and his death on February 24 demand full transparency. A vulnerable refugee with severe disabilities should never have been left without safeguards or support. The failure to provide even a basic duty of care contributed to a preventable tragedy. Justice requires accountability and concrete measures to ensure this never happens again.”

RCUK extends its deepest condolences to Mr. Shah Alam’s wife, sons, and the wider Rohingya community. No human and refugee who has escaped persecution should face preventable harm in a country that promised protection.

Bradford, United Kingdom — 19 March 2026

The Rohingya Centre of United Kingdom (RCUK) is honoured to announce that Nicholas Koumjian, Head of the Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar (IIMM), and Kaoru Okuizumi, Deputy Head of the IIMM, will conduct an official visit to the Bradford Rohingya community on Friday, 06 March 2026.

The visit will include a formal gathering at the City Banqueting Hall, followed by a Community Reception and Iftar. This engagement marks a significant moment for Rohingya families in the United Kingdom, many of whom are survivors of decades of persecution and displacement spanning from the 1960s through to 2017.

The IIMM plays a central role in collecting, analysing, and preserving evidence of serious international crimes committed against the Rohingya people by the Myanmar military and the Arakan Army. The visit by Mr. Koumjian and Ms. Okuizumi provides an important opportunity for the community to learn more about the international justice process and to share their perspectives, concerns, and hopes for the future.

“This visit is deeply meaningful for our community,” said Mohammed Amin, CEO of RCUK.
“Justice and accountability are essential for healing, recognition, and long‑term protection. We are grateful to the IIMM for engaging directly with Rohingya families in Bradford.”

The City Hall will focus on the theme:
“Justice & Accountability: Connecting International Efforts to the Rohingya Community’s Future.”

The event also aims to strengthen understanding of the justice process, promote community engagement, and reaffirm the importance of international accountability efforts. It comes at a critical moment in the ongoing International Court of Justice case, Gambia v. Myanmar, which was initiated in 2019 to address the Rohingya genocide. In January 2026, the Court heard the merit hearing, and the case is now pending deliberations, highlighting the urgent need for continued documentation, advocacy, and community engagement in support of justice for the Rohingya people.

title: Bradford’s Rohingya Community Stands for Truth and Justice at ICJ Genocide Hearings
excerpt: Bradford, United Kingdom – The three weeks of full merits hearings concluded on 29th January 2026, on the case of the Rohingya genocide at the International Court of Justice (ICJ),…
content:
Bradford, United Kingdom – The three weeks of full merits hearings concluded on 29th January 2026, on the case of the Rohingya genocide at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), brought by The Gambia against Myanmar. The judges have heard arguments of both sides and, in what is rare for an inter-State proceeding, directly from Rohingya witnesses, some of whom traveled from the camps in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh.

RCUK pays tribute to the courage and dignity of Rohingya survivors who provided direct testimony before the Court. Their harrowing accounts reflect the lived reality of systematic violence, persecution, and destruction faced by the Rohingya people. These testimonies ensure that the truth is formally recorded in international law and cannot be denied or erased.

Mohammed Amin, CEO of RCUK, attended the proceedings and stated:
“As a survivor and representative of our people, witnessing these proceedings is deeply significant. The systematic atrocities amounting to genocide against the Rohingya people are undeniable, and justice is long overdue.”

Delegates from RCUK and members of the Rohingya community, representing one of the largest Rohingya communities in Europe based in Bradford, were present to ensure that the voices and experiences of survivors are recognised. The hearings highlighted the systematic and deliberate violence carried out by Myanmar’s military over decades, including the campaigns of the 1960s, 1978, the 1990s, and the genocidal campaign of 2017 that forced hundreds of thousands to flee to Bangladesh.

The Rohingya community includes individuals who endured decades of displacement in refugee camps before resettlement in the United Kingdom under UNHCR programmes, as well as more recent arrivals who survived the 2017 atrocities. For these survivors, the ICJ proceedings represent a vital step in the ongoing struggle for truth, accountability, and protection.

The hearings centred the experiences of Rohingya men, women, and children, highlighting sexual and gender-based violence, mass killings, and forced displacement as evidence of genocidal intent. The courage of survivors who testified reflects their resilience and commitment to truth, despite ongoing risks and threats.

RCUK expresses its gratitude to The Gambia, its legal team, international partners, intervening states, civil society, and supporters worldwide who have stood with the Rohingya people. The protection and dignity of survivors and witnesses must remain a priority, and no one should face intimidation or reprisals for participating in these proceedings.

As the Court begins deliberations, RCUK calls on the international community to ensure that Myanmar complies with its obligations under international law, that provisional measures are enforced, and that meaningful accountability is achieved. For the Rohingya community in Bradford and across the diaspora, this case represents the pursuit of recognition, justice, and an end to decades of impunity.

RCUK will continue to stand with survivors and the global Rohingya community in demanding truth, justice, and lasting peace.

title: Rohingya Youth and Community Leadership: Shaping the Future of Rohingya Education
excerpt: Today, as the global education community marks the International Day of Education, the Rohingya Centre of the United Kingdom (RCUK) joins this moment to reaffirm the central role of youth…
content:
Today, as the global education community marks the International Day of Education, the Rohingya Centre of the United Kingdom (RCUK) joins this moment to reaffirm the central role of youth and communities in advancing inclusive, equitable, and quality education particularly in contexts of displacement, statelessness, and prolonged exclusion.

For the Rohingya people, access to education has been systematically denied for generations. Restrictions on movement, language, accreditation, and progression to higher education have created one of the most severe and protracted education crises in the world. Despite these conditions, Rohingya communities have sustained learning through community-led initiatives, often in the absence of formal state-supported systems.

There could not be a more fitting moment to place Rohingya youth and community leadership at the centre of education decision making. For the first time, Rohingya communities across refugee camps, host countries, and the diaspora are collectively working towards a Rohingya Education System. This is a community-led, rights-based framework designed to ensure continuity, quality, cultural relevance, and future recognition for Rohingya learners. This marks a significant shift from fragmented and temporary responses towards a coherent, long-term education vision rooted in community ownership.

This moment is also forward-looking. As the world enters the final phase of SDG 4 and begins shaping a new global education agenda, the lived experiences of stateless and displaced communities must inform future policy and practice. Education systems developed without the meaningful participation of affected communities risk reinforcing exclusion. Education systems built collaboratively with youth and communities can foster dignity, agency, and sustainable impact.

Education systems are meaningful when Rohingya youth and communities shape them

Rohingya youth leadership has grown steadily across community learning centres, refugee camps, diaspora organisations, and digital platforms. Young people are serving as educators, curriculum developers, mentors, advocates, and organisers. They are advancing inclusion, accountability, and quality within their communities, often with limited resources and institutional support.

Education is fundamentally about children and young people and their futures. For Rohingya children and young people, it is also about identity, hope, and justice. It is therefore essential that they contribute directly to the decisions that shape their learning pathways. Community-led education initiatives have long been the backbone of Rohingya education. The development of a Rohingya Education System seeks to strengthen these efforts through shared standards, coordination, and long-term vision while remaining firmly grounded in community leadership.

Yet participation remains uneven. While Rohingya youth and community actors are increasingly consulted, their engagement is rarely embedded across education design, implementation, monitoring, and evaluation. As a result, their contributions often remain informal, short-term, or disconnected from formal decision-making structures.

Encouragingly, recognition of community-led education systems is growing, particularly in displacement contexts. Education stakeholders are increasingly acknowledging the importance of local leadership in areas such as curriculum relevance, language of instruction, psychosocial well-being, inclusion, and access to secondary and higher education pathways.

When Rohingya youth and communities lead alongside education partners, the potential for inclusive, high-quality education systems built on trust, intergenerational respect, and shared responsibility can be fully realised.

Meaningful youth engagement and community leadership remain aspirational

While youth and community leadership are essential to Rohingya education, they continue to be treated as supplementary rather than structural. The priorities ahead are clear: embedding Rohingya representation within education governance; strengthening community-led systems; investing in enabling environments; and ensuring that youth and community voices shape education from vision through to evaluation.

Governments, international organisations, and education partners committed to Rohingya education should prioritise the following actions:

  • Formally recognise and support community-led education systems, including the Rohingya Education System, as legitimate and essential education pathways.
  • Embed Rohingya youth and community participation within education decision-making processes, with clear roles, safeguarding, adequate time, and transparent feedback mechanisms.
  • Engage Rohingya-led organisations not only in programme design, but also in implementation, monitoring, evaluation, and quality assurance.
  • Invest in institutional capacity-building, including teacher training, leadership development, and education governance structures.
  • Support accredited and future-oriented education pathways, including access to secondary and higher education, to ensure continuity and long-term opportunity for Rohingya learners.

A call to strengthen community-led Rohingya education

The development of a Rohingya Education System reflects decades of community resilience and a collective determination to move beyond fragmented and temporary solutions. Rohingya communities are not starting from zero, they are formalising, strengthening, and sustaining education systems they have long built and maintained under extremely challenging conditions.

As the international community shapes the future of education beyond SDG 4, Rohingya voices must be central to that process, not as beneficiaries, but as partners and leaders. Education systems designed for Rohingya communities will remain insufficient. Education systems built with Rohingya youth and communities can transform futures.

On this International Day of Education, RCUK calls for renewed commitment to community-led and youth-led education so that Rohingya children and young people are not only learners, but architects of their own education system and future.

title: 78th Anniversary of Myanmar Independence: The Rohingya Struggle
excerpt: Public Statement – 4 January 2026 Today, on 4 January 1948, Burma (now Myanmar) gained independence from British colonial rule, marking a historic moment of sovereignty. For many communities, this…
content:
Public Statement – 4 January 2026

Today, on 4 January 1948, Burma (now Myanmar) gained independence from British colonial rule, marking a historic moment of sovereignty. For many communities, this day represents freedom and the promise of a nation built on equality and inclusion. For the Rohingya people of Arakan (now Rakhine State), however, the anniversary carries a more complex and serious significance.

Arakan wasinvaded and forcibly incorporated under Burmese rule in 1784, and while the region later came under British colonisation in the late 19th century, the Rohingya remained integral to the social, economic, and cultural fabric of the land. The Rohingya, whose name derives from the ancient region of Rohang (now Arakan/Rakhine State), have lived in the region for centuries and are indigenous to the land. During the early post-independence period, Rohingya and most Muslims were recognised as citizens of Burma under the 1948 Constitution and civilian administration, enjoying full rights and participating in political, social, and economic life.

This status changed drastically following the 2 March 1962 military coup led by General Ne Win. Subsequent constitutions and laws, including the 1974 Constitution and the 1982 Citizenship Act, systematically excluded Rohingya from recognition, defining citizenship in ways that rendered most Rohingya stateless. Denied citizenship, they faced restrictions on movement, education, employment, marriage, and access to basic rights, while state policies increasingly promoted discrimination and marginalisation.

The consequences of decades of exclusion and persecution culminated in mass atrocities and displacement, particularly during the 2012 communal violence and the 2017 military-led operations, which amounted to genocide, forcing hundreds of thousands into Bangladesh and leaving hundreds of thousands internally displaced. Despite repeated warnings from international bodies, including the UN Human Rights Council, Rohingya continue to face denial of basic rights, restricted access to healthcare and education, and exclusion from their ancestral homeland.

For Rohingya, Myanmar’s independence remains incomplete and unfulfilled. True independence must be measured not only by sovereignty but by the recognition, inclusion, and dignity of all peoples, regardless of ethnicity or religion.

On this 78th anniversary, the Rohingya Centre of the United Kingdom (RCUK) reaffirms its commitment to peaceful advocacy, international cooperation, and accountability under international law. We call on the international community to acknowledge the ongoing exclusion of Rohingya from their homeland and to support justice, protection, and a future in which Rohingya can return safely, live with recognised identity, and enjoy their birth rights in Arakan as indigenous people.

Independence that excludes an entire people cannot be celebrated fully. The Rohingya struggle remains a reminder of the work that remains ensuring dignity, inclusion, and justice for all in Myanmar.

Echoing this reflection, the United Council of Rohingya (UCR) organised a Myanmar Independence Day Program at Refugee Camp in Bangladesh on 4 January 2026. The program aims to reflect on the historical significance of Myanmar’s independence, promote awareness, and foster unity and dialogue within the community.

title: RCUK Welcomes ICJ Merits Hearings and Calls for Urgent Protection and Justice for the Rohingya People
excerpt: PRESS RELEASE Bradford, UK | 21 December 2025 The Rohingya Centre of United Kingdom (RCUK) notes with significance the announcement by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) that public hearings…
content:
PRESS RELEASE

Bradford, UK | 21 December 2025

The Rohingya Centre of United Kingdom (RCUK) notes with significance the announcement by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) that public hearings on the merits in the case Application of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide (The Gambia v. Myanmar) will take place from 12 to 29 January 2026 in The Hague.

RCUK welcomes this important step in a case first initiated in November 2019, and recognises the continued engagement of the international community in upholding the Genocide Convention.

We express our sincere gratitude to the United Kingdom, which, together with Canada, Denmark, France, Germany and the Netherlands, intervened in the case on 15 November 2023. More than two years later, this intervention demonstrates the UK’s steadfast commitment to accountability, international law, and the prevention of genocide. We also extend our appreciation to the Government and people of Bangladesh, who have provided protection to the Rohingya since 1978 and continue to shoulder a significant humanitarian responsibility with generosity and dignity.

These hearings carry profound meaning for Rohingya people worldwide, including those who remain displaced, fragmented, or disappeared as a result of systematic atrocities and acts of genocide committed by the Burmese military, also now by armed groups operating in the region the Arakan Army (AA). The proceedings affirm that the international community continues to recognise the severity of these crimes and the urgent need for justice, protection, and human dignity.

Today, over 1.5 million Rohingya people continue to live in precarious conditions, lacking citizenship, security, or access to basic human rights. For these communities, the ICJ hearings are more than a legal process, they represent a crucial recognition of their suffering, a step towards accountability, and a reaffirmation of their rights under international law.

RCUK respects the ICJ as the principal judicial organ of the United Nations and underscores the importance of continued support from States and international partners to uphold the rule of law, protect civilians, and provide durable solutions for displaced communities.

As stated by Mohammed Amin, Chief Executive Officer, RCUK:

“The announcement of the ICJ’s merits hearings is a significant moment for Rohingya people everywhere, particularly for those still displaced, fragmented, and missing as a result of eight years of genocide and ongoing atrocities.

We thank the United Kingdom and its partners for their intervention, and Bangladesh for its long-standing support in hosting Rohingya refugees. This hearing signals that the world has not forgotten the Rohingya, and that accountability and protection under international law remain possible.

The suffering of our people continues, and while the Court examines this case, meaningful action to protect lives, uphold dignity, and secure rights must accompany justice. The world must see the Rohingya not just as victims, but as a people entitled to safety, recognition, and humanity.”

RCUK remains committed to working with governments, civil society, and international partners to ensure justice, protection, and durable solutions for Rohingya communities.

title: RCUK Rohingya Delegation: Reflections from the 23rd Doha Forum
excerpt: From 6–8 December 2025, the Rohingya Delegation from the Rohingya Centre UK (RCUK) was honoured to attend the 23rd Doha Forum, held under the theme Diplomacy, Dialogue, Diversity. Over three…
content:
From 6–8 December 2025, the Rohingya Delegation from the Rohingya Centre UK (RCUK) was honoured to attend the 23rd Doha Forum, held under the theme Diplomacy, Dialogue, Diversity. Over three days, RCUK joined leaders, diplomats, and institutions from around the world in urgent conversations on justice, peace, and dignity.

The delegation was privileged to meet H.E. Ban Ki‑moon, former Secretary‑General of the United Nations, whose lifelong commitment to multilateralism continues to inspire. RCUK also engaged with faith leaders including Dr Omar Suleiman and Dr Ed Kessler MBE in a session on defending the UN Charter and countering hate through interfaith solidarity, a reminder of conscience in shaping inclusive futures for displaced Rohingya and other stateless communities.

At the British Ambassador’s Reception in Qatar, RCUK met Humza Yousaf, former First Minister of Scotland; H.E. Neerav Patel, British Ambassador to Qatar; and UK MPs Rushanara Ali, Iqbal Mohammad, and Naz Shah, among others. In these exchanges, RCUK emphasised the urgent need for sustained political and diplomatic advocacy for the Rohingya people, and welcomed the announcement of the UK Government and Qatar Fund for Development’s £11.2 million joint aid package for Rohingya refugees. This timely support for vulnerable families in Cox’s Bazar comes at a critical moment as resources shrink and sustainable solutions remain urgent.

Education was a central theme of RCUK’s participation. At the high‑level panel Education as Justice in Times of Crisis, chaired by Dana Al Anzy, Strategic Partnerships Manager at the Education Above All Foundation. RCUK reaffirmed that for the Rohingya, education is not charity, it is justice, dignity, and peace. Generations of Rohingya children have been denied their right to learn due to displacement and protracted crises. RCUK remains committed to advancing Rohingya‑led education systems as a foundation for justice and lasting solutions. The delegation was also pleased to meet H.E. Al Mayassa Al Thani, whose reflections on innovation and inclusive approaches from the Global South offered valuable insights into shaping more equitable responses to displacement.

A meaningful dinner with Dr Habibur Rahman, distinguished author and historian, provided profound reflections on the Rohingya journey and dignity. His scholarship and lived experience offered depth to RCUK’s understanding of the challenges ahead and reinforced the importance of documenting and elevating Rohingya history in global discourse.

Aligned with the Forum’s overarching theme “Justice in Action – Beyond Promises to Progress,” RCUK’s participation reinforced the conviction that refugee‑led voices must be central to global dialogue. For the Rohingya, systemic inequities have long undermined the rights of children and youth, denying generations their chance to learn and thrive. This is not only a developmental loss but a profound injustice.

As the Rohingya Delegation from RCUK, we return from Doha with renewed commitment to transparency, partnership, and trust‑building. We will continue to work with global actors and local communities to transform dialogue into action — advancing justice, dignity, and resilience for the Rohingya and other displaced peoples worldwide.

Education, dignity, and justice are not aspirations. They are imperatives, and they remain at the heart of RCUK’s mission.

title: Official Announcement: RCUK appoints Ian Murch to lead Finance, Advocacy & Campaigning

content:
Rohingya Centre UK (RCUK) is delighted to announce the formal confirmation of Mr. Ian Murch as Director of Campaigning, Advocacy & Finance.

This appointment follows more than a year of dedicated and impactful service as Director of Campaigning & Advocacy, during which Mr. Murch has strengthened RCUK’s strategic engagement, public advocacy, and policy work. In his expanded portfolio, he will also oversee Finance, ensuring strengthened governance and institutional development as RCUK continues to grow and advance its mission.

He has been a National Executive Member of the National Education Union (formerly NUT) since 1987, including service as National Treasurer. He has also served as Secretary of its Bradford branch. Over his career, he has played a leading role on key committees and in major national campaigns to protect public education, oppose privatisation, defend children’s rights, and promote fairness and equality.

Since 2018, Mr. Murch has worked closely with the Rohingya community in Bradford, supporting Rohingya-led education initiatives, advocacy programmes, and capacity-building efforts. His support, alongside the solidarity of the National Education Union (NEU), has been instrumental in advancing the Rohingya community’s long-held aspiration for access to formal education in the refugee camps in Bangaldesh. Without this partnership, the progress made to date including the meaningful groundwork that will enable implementation and scaling by the end of this year would not have been possible.

Beyond education, Mr. Murch has played an important role in supporting the creation of platforms for Rohingya voices and leadership, empowering the community to shape its own narrative, advocate for its rights, and strengthen its institutional capacity.

“Mohammed Amin, CEO of RCUK, said:
“I am pleased to welcome Ian Murch in his expanded role as Director of Campaigning, Advocacy & Finance. Over the past year, Ian’s dedication and leadership have made a real difference to our work. In this new role, I am confident he will continue to strengthen our advocacy, support the growth of Rohingya-led education initiatives, and ensure the voices and aspirations of the Rohingya people are represented and advanced at every level.”

Ian Murch, Director of Campaigning, Advocacy & Finance, RCUK
“In my expanded role at RCUK, I remain fully committed to supporting Rohingya-led education in the refugee camps in Bangladesh. With the help of skilled teachers from the UK and the support of the NEU, we are equipping volunteers in the camps and providing the resources they need. Working closely with the community, we aim to ensure every Rohingya child has access to education and a chance to thrive. If you want to help, please contact me at ian.m@rcuk.org.uk.”

RCUK extends its sincere appreciation to Mr. Murch for his dedication and looks forward to his continued leadership in advancing the dignity, rights, and aspirations of the Rohingya people in the UK and beyond.

title: Joint Statement Rejecting ULA/AA’s Claim to Legitimacyand Upholding Rohingya Rights and Inclusive Authority in Arakan State
excerpt: Preamble: Guided by international law, human rights principles, and the Charter of the UnitedNations, we, the undersigned representatives of Rohingya and allied civil societyorganisations worldwide, reaffirm the inherent rights of…
content:
Preamble:

Guided by international law, human rights principles, and the Charter of the United
Nations, we, the undersigned representatives of Rohingya and allied civil society
organisations worldwide, reaffirm the inherent rights of the Rohingya people and all
ethnic communities of Arakan State. The Rohingya, originating from Rohang—the
historical name of Arakan—are indigenous to the region and rightful Arakanese.

We stand for inclusive governance, peaceful coexistence, and sustainable
development across Arakan State. We categorically reject any claims or
campaigns by the United League of Arakan (ULA) and its armed wing, the Arakan
Army (AA), seeking to monopolise authority, erase Rohingya identity, or delegitimise
our historical and indigenous rights.

This statement represents the lawful and collective voice of the Rohingya people
and the broader Arakanese population, calling on the United Nations, its Member
States, and the international community to recognise and uphold these rights.

Statement of Concern:

The Rohingya, as indigenous Arakanese, have endured decades of systematic
persecution, statelessness, and mass atrocities amounting to crimes against
humanity and genocide.

In September 2025, the ULA/AA and associated entities submitted appeals seeking
recognition as the governing authority in Arakan. We firmly reject these appeals, as
the ULA/AA does not represent the Rohingya people. While the AA publicly claims
that Muslims and minorities enjoy new freedoms under its rule, verified testimonies
and independent reports demonstrate the opposite.

According to the Fortify Rights report dated 23 July 2025, the AA is responsible for
widespread abductions, brutal torture, and the murder of Rohingya men and
women—some of whom were found beheaded—in flagrant violation of
international law. Furthermore, the UN Report (A/HRC/60/20) confirms that AA
fighters shelled and burned Rohingya villages in Buthidaung and Maungdaw
between May and August 2024. These acts reveal the conduct of a perpetrator, not
a protector.

Rejecting the ULA/AA does not imply support for the Burmese military junta, which
has also committed grave atrocities and continues to conceal its genocidal crimes.
Both actors must be held accountable under international law.

Legal and Humanitarian Implications:

Recognition of ULA/AA would seriously undermine ongoing investigations into war
crimes and crimes against humanity. Justice requires that accountability be
pursued through established international mechanisms, including the International
Criminal Court (ICC) and International Court of Justice (ICJ).

The international community must refrain from legitimising any armed group
involved in gross human rights violations and war crimes, regardless of political
context or justification.

Vision for Arakan:

We advocate for all ethnicities in Arakan State including the Rohingya, Rakhine,
Kamein, Mru, and other indigenous communities to enjoy full political
representation, equal rights, and shared autonomy within a peaceful and inclusive
governance framework.

This recognises all Arakanese peoples as equal stakeholders in the region’s future,
committed to coexistence, justice, and long-term stability in Arakan State.

We urge the ULA/AA to:

Immediately cease all acts of violence, forced conscription, and targeted
attacks against Rohingya civilians;

  • Acknowledge and take accountability for the crimes committed against Rohingya peoples;
  • Engage sincerely in dialogue aimed at reconciliation, justice, and inclusive governance;
  • Work collaboratively with Rohingya and all ethnic communities to build an Arakan that belongs to all its people.

Arakan is the shared homeland of all its sons and daughters. It must not become an instrument of dictatorship, militarisation, or ethnic domination. There will be no genuine peace, unity, or stability in Arakan without justice, equality, and full rights for the Rohingya people.

Call to the International Community:

We call upon the United Nations, Member States, and diplomatic missions to:

  • Reject any claim by the ULA/AA to legitimate governance in Arakan;
  • Support the establishment of an inclusive, representative governance framework that respects all ethnic communities;
  • Refrain from recognising or engaging with armed groups implicated in war crimes or ongoing human rights violations;
  • Support all efforts aimed at achieving justice, reconciliation, and durable peace for every community in Arakan.

The Arakanese peoples including the indigenous Rohingya deserve justice,
protection, and the right to return to their ancestral lands in safety and dignity.

title: From Refugee Camps to the British Army: The Inspiring Journey of Ismail Mohammed
excerpt: The Rohingya Centre UK (RCUK) shares the stories of Rohingya families who, after being forced to flee their homeland, have found sanctuary and new beginnings in Britain. Today we are…
content:
The Rohingya Centre UK (RCUK) shares the stories of Rohingya families who, after being forced to flee their homeland, have found sanctuary and new beginnings in Britain. Today we are proud to highlight the remarkable journey of Ismail Mohammed, a proud member of the British Army and a graduate of Law (LL.B) and LL.M , who grew up in Manningham, Bradford.

A Family’s Journey to Safety

Ismail’s family were among the thousands of Rohingya forced to flee from Myanmar in the 1990s due to persecution. For 18 long years, they endured life in refugee camps in Bangladesh, where access to education, healthcare and opportunities was scarce.

In 2008, through the UK Resettlement Programme, they were offered the chance to rebuild their lives in Bradford. Ismail arrived aged just 10, unable to speak English and adjusting to an entirely new culture.

With resilience and determination, supported by teachers, mentors, family and his community, he excelled in his studies. In 2022 he proudly graduated with Bachelor of Laws LL.B (Hons) from the University of Bradford, followed by an LL.M in International Humans Laws from the University of Leeds, before going on to serve in the British Army, making both his family and his country proud.

Words of Appreciation

Ismail Mohammed says:
“I am forever grateful to Britain and to the people of Bradford. This country gave my family safety and gave me the chance to study, grow, and contribute. Education has transformed my life, and I wish for every Rohingya child in the camps to be given the same opportunity.”

His father, Harun Mohammed, reflects:
“We spent nearly two decades in refugee camps with little hope. To now see my son as a graduate and serving soldier in the British Army is beyond what I could ever have dreamed of. Britain gave us protection, dignity, and a future. For that, we are truly thankful.”

The Power of Education

Ismail’s journey demonstrates the resilience of Rohingya youth and the transformative power of education. His story is living proof of the value of Britain’s humanitarian commitments — turning despair into opportunity and ensuring that young people not only survive but thrive.

This is why RCUK is leading the way with a Rohingya-led, sustainable, high-quality, internationally accredited education programme. Rooted in the heritage of the Rohingya people of Rohang (Arakan), this initiative aims to provide children in refugee camps with the same chance to learn, achieve, and contribute positively to society.

Amin Mohammed, CEO of RCUK, states:
“Ismail’s story is a testimony to what can be achieved when refugees are given safety, education and opportunity. At RCUK, we are building a model of education that is led by Rohingya, for Rohingya, to ensure every child can fulfil their potential. Education is not just a right, it is the key to dignity, stability, and hope for the future.”

The Rohingya Centre UK welcomes testimonies and personal journeys. To contribute your story, please write to us at: info@rcuk.org.uk

title: Statement from the Rohingya Centre UK on the UN High-Level Conference on the Situation of Rohingya Muslims and Other Minorities in Myanmar
excerpt: New York – 30 September 2025, The Rohingya Centre UK (RCUK) welcomes the convening of the United Nations High-Level Conference on the situation of Rohingya Muslims and other minorities in…
content:
New York – 30 September 2025,

The Rohingya Centre UK (RCUK) welcomes the convening of the United Nations High-Level Conference on the situation of Rohingya Muslims and other minorities in Myanmar. We commend the engagement of over 70 countries, international agencies, and civil society organisations, and extend our appreciation to the people and the leadership of Bangladesh, the Honourable Chief Adviser, Professor Mohammed Yunus for hosting Rohingya refugees.

We also welcome the renewed humanitarian commitments announced by the United Kingdom, the United States, and other UN member states during the conference. This support remains essential to sustaining the lives of more than 1.2 million Rohingya in Bangladesh, who continue to face worsening restrictions, shrinking aid, insecurity, and a pervasive climate of fear. Yet, while humanitarian assistance is indispensable, it cannot substitute for justice, dignity, and durable solutions.

As many underlined, the resolution of the Rohingya crisis must be found within Myanmar. This requires the establishment of safe and protected areas in Arakan (Rakhine State), with robust international monitoring, to create the conditions for the voluntary, safe, dignified, and sustainable return of Rohingya refugees. It also demands an immediate end to impunity, genuine accountability for atrocities, and the full inclusion of the Rohingya as equal citizens with guaranteed rights and protections.

Lasting peace and stability in Myanmar depend on a sustainable resolution rooted in trust-building, inclusivity, and the protection of fundamental rights for all communities.

At the conference, Rohingya youth voice Maung Sawyedullah, now a student at New York University, delivered a powerful testimony: “Without self-determination for the Rohingya and international protection in Arakan, there can be no lasting peace. Any initiative about the Rohingya that excludes Rohingya refugees themselves from decision-making to nation-building—is unsustainable and unjust. We are not just victims; we have the potential to make a difference.”

His words reflect a wider truth: education is not a privilege but a necessity for Rohingya survival, resilience, and empowerment. It echoes the aspirations of countless Rohingya children and youth striving to learn, develop skills, and build self-reliance and seeking to become part of the solution rather than remain perpetually dependent on aid.

In response to this urgent need, RCUK has introduced the Rohingya Education Board, a comprehensive Rohingya-led system designed to deliver meaningful, high-quality, and internationally accredited education for Rohingya children and youth. It will also create pathways to higher learning, foster leadership, and strengthen resilience within the community. During 7–17 September 2025, an RCUK delegation representing the UK, US, Germany, and the Netherlands visited the refugee camps in Bangladesh. Engaging directly with community members, teachers, students, and youth, the delegation found overwhelming support for this initiative as a vital step toward restoring hope and opportunity.

As Ian Murch, Campaigns and Advocacy Director of RCUK, stated: “We deeply appreciate the UK’s £27 million funding for food, shelter, clean water, and other life-saving services for half a million Rohingya refugees. Yet, what remains critically missing is education. The United Kingdom has the opportunity to support this initiative at a relatively small cost—an investment that would transform the future for an entire people.”

We therefore call upon Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office, and other UN member states to support and fund Rohingya-led initiatives such as the Education Board that are sustainable, cost-effective, and community-driven. We also urge Bangladesh to enact meaningful policy reforms to enable education and livelihood opportunities, and call on international aid organisations to enhance efficiency and accountability in the delivery of resources.

The path forward requires more than simply keeping the Rohingya people alive. It requires empowering them to live with dignity, to participate fully in society, and to contribute to a future of peace and stability in Myanmar.

The Rohingya Centre UK reaffirms its readiness to work with UN member states, international partners, and our Rohingya community worldwide to advance a collective vision of justice, dignity, and durable solutions for all.
